record.title: China's cybersecurity standards committee publishes AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0 with an agent lifecycle risk and control model
record.summary: On 2026-09-14, China’s National Technical Committee 260 on Cybersecurity (TC260), under CAC guidance, published the Chinese-language AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0. Its 136-page document classifies risks and recommends mitigations across AI-agent design, installation/deployment, instruction input, reasoning/planning, tool execution, memory, output and shutdown. It identifies prompt injection, context overflow, tool poisoning and overreach, memory contamination/theft, behavior escape, and residual credentials/processes after shutdown. Recommended controls include pre-deployment risk assessment, staged increases in access and autonomy, unique agent identity and least privilege, revocable credentials, human approval and ability to interrupt high-risk operations, fail-closed approval handling, runtime guardrails, and memory isolation. Comparison with the official 2025 Framework 2.0 shows that 2.0 already discussed autonomous agent planning and privilege/file-access risks, but did not have a dedicated agentic-AI lifecycle appendix. Version 3.0 adds that appendix and separately maps agent identity/permission, planning, tool-execution, memory, embodied and multi-agent risks. This documents a change in framework scope; neither publication establishes binding law, broad adoption or control effectiveness.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_PUBLICATION_EVENT
claims.text: TC260 published AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0 on 2026-09-14 under CAC guidance.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_DOCUMENT_CONTENT
claims.text: The framework describes agent risks across design, deployment, instruction input, reasoning/planning, tool execution, memory, output and shutdown.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_DOCUMENT_RECOMMENDATIONS
claims.text: The framework recommends staged access/autonomy increases, unique identities and least privilege, revocable credentials, human review and interruption for high-risk operations, fail-closed approval, runtime controls, and memory protections.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The framework changes deployment practices, is binding law, or has measurably improved safety in use.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_VERSION_COMPARISON
claims.text: Framework 2.0 already identifies autonomous AI-agent planning, access to files/permissions/interfaces/tools, privilege-abuse risks and risk grading. Framework 3.0 adds a dedicated Agentic AI risk-management appendix and separately classifies identity/permission misuse, reasoning/planning, tool invocation/execution, memory storage and embodied/multi-agent risks.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED_DOCUMENT_STRUCTURE
claims.text: Framework 2.0 includes an agent definition in its glossary and a general risk-grading appendix; Framework 3.0 includes a stand-alone agentic-AI lifecycle risk-management appendix and retains risk grading using application scenario, intelligence level and application scale.

evidence_gaps.description: Version 3.0's exact additions and deletions relative to the full version 2.0 text have not been established.
No independent evidence shows how many providers or deployers adopted the recommendations or whether the controls reduced agent-security incidents.
The legal or compliance status of Framework 3.0 is not stated in the inspected release notice or framework passages.

brief.importance_rationale: If the published framework is used by implementers, its explicit agent lifecycle controls can change local design and deployment-review choices for identity, permissions, memory, tool use and human intervention. Score 4 reflects meaningful engineering and governance consequence while capping for unverified adoption, effectiveness, binding force and exact novelty relative to version 2.0.
limitations: The release describes a technical framework; the inspected pages do not establish that its recommendations are binding legal requirements.
No organizational adoption, enforcement, compliance cost, incident reduction or safety effectiveness evidence was inspected.
The framework's risk descriptions are policy statements and anticipated risks, not independent empirical prevalence measurements.
The version comparison is a targeted text-level comparison of selected agent, risk-classification and appendix sections, not a clause-by-clause legal or bilingual translation audit.
brief.summary: On 2026-09-14, China’s National Technical Committee 260 on Cybersecurity (TC260), under CAC guidance, published the Chinese-language AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0. Its 136-page document classifies risks and recommends mitigations across AI-agent design, installation/deployment, instruction input, reasoning/planning, tool execution, memory, output and shutdown. It identifies prompt injection, context overflow, tool poisoning and overreach, memory contamination/theft, behavior escape, and residual credentials/processes after shutdown. technical.claimed_result: The release describes the framework as updating risk classifications and optimizing technical response and comprehensive governance measures to improve shared understanding and risk response. These are the issuing body's stated aims, not measured outcomes.
technical.demonstrated_result: The primary document contains a structured agent risk taxonomy and these control recommendations (Chinese PDF pp.37–48; PDF pages 41–52 in the web-rendered file, with specific text at lines 981–1137). This demonstrates what the framework recommends, not that any system implements or benefits from the controls.
technical.implementation_status: TC260 announced Framework 3.0 on 2026-09-14. The official 136-page bilingual 3.0 PDF and official 92-page bilingual 2.0 PDF were both text-inspected for this targeted comparison. No implementation audit was attempted.
technical.mechanism: The document treats agent security as a lifecycle problem and recommends layered controls: pre-use risk review; incremental increases in access/autonomy; unique identities and least privilege; revocable credentials; safety checks on tools, skills and their metadata; human approval and interruptibility at high-risk decision points; runtime monitoring and fail-closed handling; segmented memory with limited retention; and cleanup/revocation when the agent is retired.
technical.regime: Chinese-language national cybersecurity technical guidance for AI R&D, deployment and use, including agentic systems; applicability, legal force and adoption by organizations are not established by the inspected release materials.
technical.reproducibility: Not an experimental result. The claims about document content are directly inspectable in the primary PDF; adoption and control effectiveness require separate evidence.
technical.strongest_baseline: The official 2025 Framework 2.0 already mentions autonomous agent planning, access to files/permissions/interfaces/tools, privilege abuse, application risk grading and an agent glossary definition. Framework 3.0 adds a dedicated Agentic AI risk-management appendix and explicit categories for identity/permission, planning, invocation/execution, memory, embodied and multi-agent risks.

brief.title: China's cybersecurity standards committee publishes AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0 with an agent lifecycle risk and control model
brief.why_it_matters: The framework translates agent security concerns into a lifecycle control set spanning identity, permissions, tool supply chains, untrusted inputs, long-term memory, human intervention and shutdown. If implemented, these recommendations could change agent platform architecture and deployment review. The consequence is bounded because this is a guidance document and no adoption, enforcement, or control effectiveness was established.
